blocks.prompt: The Moose That Grows a New Crown Every Year
blocks.text: A moose is the biggest deer in the world. A big one weighs as much as a small car. Only the boy moose grows antlers. They spread out wide and flat, like two big hands on his head. Here is the strange part. Every winter, the antlers fall off. They just drop into the snow. In the spring, the moose grows a whole new pair. He does this again and again, every single year of his life. A moose can swim. He can put his head under the water and pull up plants to eat.

blocks.prompt: The Antlers That Grow Back Every Spring
blocks.text: A male moose is called a bull. A big bull stands taller at the shoulder than a grown man and can weigh 1,500 pounds. On his head he carries antlers that spread as wide as your arms twice over. Those antlers are made of real bone, and they are brand new every year. In the spring, the bone starts pushing out of his skull. It grows fast, sometimes an inch in a day, covered in a soft fuzzy skin called velvet that feeds it blood. By late summer the antlers are finished. The velvet dries and peels off, and the bull rubs the antlers on trees to clean them. He uses them in the fall to show off and to shove other bulls out of the way. Then winter comes and he drops them. They fall right off in the snow. Mice and squirrels chew them up for the minerals inside. In the spring, he starts all over again.

blocks.prompt: Built for the Cold North
blocks.text: Look at a moose and the first thing you notice is that the proportions seem wrong. The legs are too long. The shoulders hump up too high. The nose droops like it was borrowed from a larger animal. But every one of those odd parts is doing a job. The legs come first. A moose steps over deep snow instead of plowing through it, and it wades chest deep into ponds without swimming. Long legs cost it something, though: a moose cannot easily reach the grass at its feet. So it does not graze the way a cow does. It browses, stripping leaves, buds, and twigs from shrubs and young trees at head height. That habit gave the animal its name. The word moose comes from an Algonquian word meaning something close to he strips it off, a name given by people who watched moose peel bark from trees. The nose is doing science of its own. A moose can close its nostrils, dunk its whole head, and feel around underwater for pond plants. It eats those plants for a reason beyond hunger. Water plants are loaded with sodium, which is scarce in the leaves and twigs the moose eats the rest of the year. A moose diving in a pond is not being playful. It is refilling its salt supply. Even the huge ears are working. A moose sees poorly, but it hears and smells extremely well, and researchers have tested whether the wide flat antlers help funnel sound toward the ears. Nothing about a moose is decoration. It is a machine for surviving a long, cold, snowy winter.

blocks.prompt: The Most Expensive Hat in the Forest
blocks.text: Every spring, a bull moose starts building something absurd. Out of two bony bases on his skull, new antlers begin to push upward. They are living bone, sheathed in velvet, a furred skin threaded with blood vessels that feeds the growth. And they grow fast. Antler is the fastest growing tissue of any mammal on Earth, capable of adding close to an inch of bone in a single day. By late summer the bull is carrying a rack that can span six feet and weigh forty pounds. Then he lets the blood supply die, scrapes the dried velvet off against a tree, and walks into fall wearing forty pounds of polished bone. Consider the cost. All that calcium and phosphorus has to come from somewhere, and it comes out of his own skeleton and his food. He burns energy carrying it. He snags it on branches. And then, a few months later, he throws it away. Special cells eat away the base until the antlers simply drop off in the snow. Mice, squirrels, and porcupines gnaw the fallen bone for minerals, which is why you almost never find a shed antler lying whole in the woods. Come spring, he starts over. Why build something so expensive and then discard it? Because antlers are not weapons first. They are advertisements. A bull cannot lie about his antlers. Only a healthy, well fed, genetically strong animal can afford to grow a huge rack in a single summer, so the rack is honest proof of his condition. Rival bulls read it from across a clearing and often back down without fighting at all. Cows read it too. In the language of biology, this is called an honest signal, and it works precisely because it is costly. A cheap advertisement any weak bull could fake would tell nobody anything. So the moose pays, every year, in bone and calories, for a message that cannot be forged. Then he drops the message in the snow and grows a new one.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Moose That Grows a New Crown Every Year

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Alces alces, the largest living deer
Antler bone grows up to an inch per day
Cold adapted: it overheats above about 57°F in summer
Winter ticks can number in the tens of thousands on one animal
Brainworm spreads to moose from white-tailed deer
Range is shifting north as winters warm

blocks.prompt: The Giant That Cannot Take Its Coat Off
blocks.text: The moose is the largest deer that has ever lived through to the present day, and almost everything about it is an answer to the same question: how do you survive winter? The answers are elegant. Legs long enough to step over snowpack rather than wade through it. A dense two layer coat with hollow guard hairs that trap air and float the animal when it swims. A digestive system that can extract a living from frozen twigs. A body big enough that it loses heat slowly, because volume grows faster than surface area. Every one of those adaptations is a bet on cold. And that is the problem, because the bet is now going the wrong way. A moose is superbly insulated and cannot take the coat off. Above roughly 57 degrees Fahrenheit in summer, it begins to suffer heat stress. It stops feeding, seeks shade or water, and eats less at exactly the time of year it should be laying down fat. A moose entering winter underweight is a moose in trouble. Then there is the tick. Winter ticks latch onto moose calves by the thousands, sometimes tens of thousands on a single animal. The moose grooms frantically, rubbing off patches of its own insulating hair, and the ticks drink enough blood to leave calves anemic. Here is the cruel machinery: tick larvae wait on vegetation in the fall, and a long warm autumn with late snow gives them more time to find a host. Warmer springs let the engorged females drop onto bare ground instead of snow, which is where they survive to lay eggs. Milder weather does not just make the moose uncomfortable. It manufactures more ticks. A third pressure arrives on four legs. White-tailed deer carry a parasite called brainworm that does them almost no harm. As winters soften, deer expand north into moose country and bring it with them. In a moose, brainworm is frequently fatal. None of this is a story about a weak animal. The moose is a masterpiece of cold weather engineering, and it is being undone by a few degrees, which is a particular kind of failure worth understanding. Specialists win decisively in the conditions they were built for, and they have nowhere to go when those conditions move. Moose populations in the southern edge of their range, in New Hampshire, Vermont, and Minnesota, have fallen sharply. Farther north, in Alaska and across Canada, moose are pushing into shrubland that used to be tundra. The species is not vanishing. It is retreating, and it is leaving the map it once held.
